Does clone-censor-weighting carry modelling bias?

Modelling-bias QBA on two public CCW datasets: Maringe lung cancer vs SynPUF MI cohort

Author

Artis Luguzis

Published

October 5, 2026

ImportantKey answer

Modelling bias in CCW depends on the study: it appears in the small Maringe study, not in the larger SynPUF study. In each dataset the true effect was set to the observed CCW estimate, and the study was replayed 5,000 times on the original patients. A separate set of replays checked the case of no treatment effect.

Maringe lung cancer (n = 200, 48 deaths) SynPUF MI cohort (n = 1,590, 578 events)
Observed CCW HR (95% CI) 0.62 (0.37–1.04) 0.87 (0.63–1.20)
Bias, log-HR (MC 95% interval) -0.018 (-0.030 to -0.005) -0.002 (-0.014 to 0.010)
Bias as % of one SE 6% 1%
95% CI coverage (target 95%) 93.7% 94.7%
Type I error (target 5%) 7.3% 5.4%
Corrected HR (95% CI), calibrated p 0.63 (0.37–1.08), p = 0.10 0.87 (0.63–1.20), p = 0.41

Monte Carlo SE: about 0.3 percentage points for coverage and type I error. Bold cells differ from target by more than their Monte Carlo error.

  • Maringe: small point-estimate bias (HR 1.7% too favourable to surgery), CIs that under-cover, and a type I error inflated by about half. The analysis is not centred on HR = 1 even with unlimited data.
  • SynPUF: no detectable bias, nominal coverage, and a type I error close to 5%. QBA passes this analysis.
  • For the paper: this is a stronger demonstration than one dataset. It shows that modelling-bias QBA separates a problematic analysis from a sound one — the study-specific check the draft argues for.

1. What was done

The draft paper’s steps, applied to the published CCW analysis of each dataset:

Paper step What it means here
1. Fit the reference model Run each dataset’s CCW analysis (Section 1.1).
2. Keep baseline data All covariates and each patient’s actual treatment date are kept unchanged.
3. Predict outcomes New event times from a Weibull model fitted to each dataset, in which treatment changes the hazard from the day it starts. Treatment happens only if the patient has not had the event by that date. The treatment effect is calibrated so that the true CCW effect equals the observed estimate.
4. Repeat 5,000 replays per scenario; two scenarios per dataset: observed effect and no effect (20,000 CCW analyses; 6 failed).
5. Re-analyse The same CCW function as on the real data.
6. Quantify Bias, CI coverage, type I error, each with Monte Carlo SE.
7. Adjust Bias-corrected estimate, widened CI, simulation-calibrated p-value.

1.1 The two datasets

Maringe et al. (2020) Webster-Clark et al. (2025)

Patients / events 200 / 48 deaths in 1 year 1,590 / 578 readmissions or deaths in 180 days
Treated (per strategy window) 106 operated within 6 months (42 on day 1) 218 started within 30 days, 541 within 90 days
Contrast Surgery within 6 months vs no surgery within 6 months Start within 90 days vs within 30 days of discharge (tutorial’s main contrast)
Censoring weights Control arm: Cox model for time to surgery (7 covariates). Surgery arm: logistic model for surgery by 6 months among survivors Logistic model at the window end (age, sex, renal disease), up-weighting only those who started in the last 7 days of the window (tutorial method)

2. How the simulation works (methods note)

Can we “simulate under CCW”? Yes, but the patients are simulated, not the CCW. CCW is an analysis procedure (cloning, artificial censoring, censoring weights, weighted outcome model), not a model of how outcomes arise, so nothing can be drawn from it directly:

  • The fitted CCW outcome model describes survival under two strategies: every patient appears in both arms, with one hazard ratio applying from day 0. A real patient has one history, and before treatment both strategies are identical for that patient, so a hazard that differs between arms during the grace period cannot generate real data.
  • The cloned dataset is not data: clones, artificial censoring and weights are produced by the analysis. Redrawing outcomes on the clones with weights held fixed makes the artificial censoring non-informative and the weights irrelevant. That would test only a weighted Cox fit, not CCW.

So each outcome-generating model is a patient-level model fitted to the original data: Weibull survival with treatment as a time-varying exposure, h(t) = h₀(t)·exp(γ′X + θ·1{t ≥ treatment date}). Covariates, treatment dates and early loss to follow-up are kept (paper Step 2). New event times are drawn from this model. Each simulated dataset therefore looks like the original data, and the whole CCW procedure is re-run on it.

Why the truth is not θ. θ is the effect of treatment once received, at fixed covariates. The CCW hazard ratio compares strategies, and differs from θ for three reasons:

  1. Grace-period dilution. Patients spend the time from day 0 to their treatment date untreated. Early on, both arms share the same hazard.
  2. Non-proportional hazards. The strategy hazard ratio changes over time, so a single Cox HR is a weighted average that depends on when events occur.
  3. Marginal versus conditional. The CCW model contains the strategy only, and hazard ratios do not collapse over covariates.

None of these has a closed form, so the truth ψ(θ) is computed numerically: the base data are copied to about 50,000 patients (same covariate mix and treatment timing), outcomes are simulated, and the same CCW function is run; this is repeated 24 times and averaged. With that much data the small-sample bias is gone, and averaging removes the random error. What remains is the value CCW targets.

Calibration (paper Step 3). θ is then searched until ψ(θ) equals the observed CCW estimate, so the truth is “the CCW model parameter”:

Dataset Fitted θ Calibrated θ* Observed CCW log-HR Truth ψ(θ*) Truth MCSE Search steps
Maringe -0.41 -0.70 -0.477 -0.477 0.005 4
SynPUF -0.03 0.66 -0.138 -0.147 0.006 3

The final truth (24 datasets) agrees with the observed estimate within Monte Carlo error of the search, which used 12 datasets per step.

In SynPUF the fitted treatment effect is about zero, which fits the tutorial’s note that the synthetic data break the treatment–outcome link. To reproduce the observed HR of 0.87 for “within 90 vs within 30 days”, the calibrated world needs a harmful treatment (θ* = 0.66): starting later then looks better. The exact value of θ* does not matter for the QBA. What matters is that the true CCW effect equals the observed one.

Type I error: a separate scenario with θ = 0. Treatment is given no effect while all covariate effects are kept, and the study is replayed with the same random numbers. Here every patient’s outcome is identical under both strategies, so every estimand is null at once: conditional and marginal HR, strategy HR, risk differences. The truth is exactly log-HR = 0 and needs no estimation. The large-sample value ψ(0) is still computed, but only as a diagnostic: it shows how far CCW is off-centre even with unlimited data (Maringe -0.041, SynPUF 0.014).

3. Results: the two datasets side by side

Maringe. The average estimate is HR 0.61 instead of 0.62: a bias of -0.018, away from the null and detectable, but small (6% of one SE). The robust SE is 3.9% too small, so coverage is 93.7%. With no surgery effect, 7.3% of studies are significant: 6.1% in favour of surgery and only 1.2% against it. Even with unlimited data the null CCW HR would be 0.96, most likely because the censoring models do not fully capture how surgery decisions depend on patient characteristics. A 5% test would need |z| > 2.16 instead of 1.96.

SynPUF. The average estimate is HR 0.86 against a truth of 0.86 (bias -0.002, MC 95% interval -0.014 to 0.010). The robust SE matches the true variability (relative error 0.3%), coverage is 94.7% and type I error 5.4% (MCSE 0.3%), with false positives evenly split between directions. Under no effect the large-sample offset is small (0.014).

Why the difference? The two analyses differ in several ways at once, so this demo cannot say which one matters:

  • size and number of events (48 vs 578 events);
  • the contrast (treatment vs no treatment, against two treatment windows that share most of their patients);
  • the weighting method (Cox model vs logistic model at the window end);
  • the dataset itself.

The paper’s discussion predicts that small samples carry the highest risk, which is consistent with what we see. A sub-sampling run (SynPUF reduced to 200 patients) would separate size from design.

4. Correction of the observed results (paper Step 7)

Dataset Observed HR (95% CI) Observed p Corrected HR (95% CI) Calibrated p 5% critical |z|
Maringe 0.62 (0.37–1.04) 0.072 0.63 (0.37–1.08) 0.100 2.16
SynPUF 0.87 (0.63–1.20) 0.398 0.87 (0.63–1.20) 0.406 2.00

Correction: corrected estimate = observed estimate − bias (the paper’s grid search, to first order). The CI is widened by empirical SE / model SE where the model SE is too small. The calibrated p-value is the share of no-effect replays with |z| at least as large as observed. Neither conclusion changes. The Maringe evidence is weaker than the naive analysis suggests; the SynPUF result needs no correction.

5. Alignment with the draft paper

Draft paper What the demo shows
Abstract: “even an established statistical method such as clone-censor weighting may be affected by modelling bias” Supported, with nuance: affected in Maringe, not in SynPUF. The word “may” is right, and the comparison is a good illustration of why the check must be study-specific.
ISPE 2026 remark (Wang, Zivich et al.): CCW may have low 95% CI coverage Partly supported: under-coverage in Maringe (93.7%), nominal in SynPUF.
Discussion, high-risk use cases (small samples, complex methods) Consistent: the small study shows the problems, the larger one does not (confounded with design; see Section 3).
Section 2.3: set the true effect to the original estimate Works, but needs a calibration step for CCW, because the outcome-generating model cannot be the CCW model itself (methods note). Suggested sentence for 2.3: “If the analysis estimand differs from the generating parameter (e.g. CCW, marginal estimands), the true value is the large-sample value of the analysis, and the generating parameter is calibrated to it.”
Section 2.6: type I error from a separate null simulation Essential, and the simplest scenario: with no effect every estimand is exactly null, so no truth needs to be estimated. In Maringe it revealed the offset that persists with unlimited data, which the observed-effect scenario alone cannot show.
Section 2.7: correction Demonstrated for both datasets; with one observed-effect scenario, “observed − bias” is the paper’s grid search to first order.
Discussion, limitation 2: QBA assumes the model is correct Nuance worth adding: because real treatment dates are kept, a weight model that does not capture treatment decisions is detected through the null scenario.
Section 2.4: 10,000 repetitions Feasible: this run (20,000 CCW analyses plus calibration and large-sample truths) took about 17 minutes on 2 cores.

6. Caveats and next steps

  • B = 5,000 per scenario (paper: 10,000). The truths are simulated (MCSE about 0.005), already included in the bias intervals.
  • 6 of 20,000 analyses failed (all SynPUF: “aeqSurv exception, an interval has effective length 0”). A simulated event fell within numerical tolerance of a window boundary. This is an artefact of continuous simulated times against day-level data, and rounding simulated times to days would remove it.
  • SynPUF is analysed with an HR rather than the tutorial’s 180-day risk difference, so the tutorial’s exact estimand is not tested.
  • Next: sub-sample SynPUF to n = 200 to separate sample size from design; check the Maringe null offset with a more flexible censoring model; bootstrap CIs; verification step; B = 10,000.

A3. Data-generating mechanism

Kept fixed from the original data (paper Step 2): covariates XiX_i, each patient’s treatment date sis_i (si=∞s_i = \infty if never treated), and censoring time CiC_i. For Maringe Ci=365.24C_i = 365.24; for SynPUF CiC_i is the observed time for the 30 patients lost to follow-up before day 180, otherwise 180.

Outcome model. Weibull proportional hazards with treatment as a time-varying exposure:

hi(t)=λρtρ−1exp⁡{γ⊤Xi+θI(t≥si)},ηi=log⁡λ+γ⊤Xi,h_i(t) = \lambda \rho\, t^{\rho - 1} \exp\{\gamma^\top X_i + \theta\, I(t \ge s_i)\}, \qquad \eta_i = \log\lambda + \gamma^\top X_i,

Hi(t)=eηi[min(t,si)ρ+eθmax{0,tρ−siρ}].H_i(t) = e^{\eta_i}\left[\min(t, s_i)^{\rho} + e^{\theta}\,\max\{0,\; t^{\rho} - s_i^{\rho}\}\right].

It is fitted to the original data by maximum likelihood, ℓ=∑i[δiloghi(Yi)−Hi(Yi)]\ell = \sum_i \left[\delta_i \log h_i(Y_i) - H_i(Y_i)\right]; the fitted values are in Table A3. In simulation, log⁡λ\log\lambda, ρ\rho and γ\gamma are kept at their fitted values and θ\theta is set to the scenario value (θ*\theta^* or 0).

Simulation by inversion (common random numbers: UiU_i depends only on the replicate seed, not on θ\theta). With Ei=−log⁡UiE_i = -\log U_i, Ui∼Uniform(0,1)U_i \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1):

Ti={(Eie−ηi)1/ρif Ei≤eηisiρ (event before treatment),{siρ+(Ei−eηisiρ)e−ηi−θ}1/ρotherwise.T_i = \begin{cases} \left(E_i\, e^{-\eta_i}\right)^{1/\rho} & \text{if } E_i \le e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho} \text{ (event before treatment)},\\[4pt] \left\{ s_i^{\rho} + \left(E_i - e^{\eta_i} s_i^{\rho}\right) e^{-\eta_i - \theta} \right\}^{1/\rho} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}

Observed data: Yi=min⁡(Ti,Ci)Y_i = \min(T_i, C_i), δi=I(Ti≤Ci)\delta_i = I(T_i \le C_i); treatment is observed at sis_i only if si≤Yis_i \le Y_i.

R code: likelihood and outcome simulation (R/dgm.R) 
#' Negative log-likelihood of the Weibull PH model with time-varying treatment
#' @param par c(alpha, log_rho, gamma, theta).
#' @param X Design matrix; @param time,status,s Follow-up, event, planned treatment time.
#' @return Scalar.
dgm_negloglik <- function(par, X, time, status, s) {
  p <- ncol(X)
  rho <- exp(par[2])
  eta <- par[1] + drop(X %*% par[2 + seq_len(p)])
  theta <- par[p + 3]
  on_trt <- s < time
  cumhaz <- exp(eta) *
    (pmin(s, time)^rho + on_trt * exp(theta) * (time^rho - pmin(s, time)^rho))
  loghaz <- log(rho) + (rho - 1) * log(time) + eta + theta * on_trt
  -sum(status * loghaz - cumhaz)
}

#' Simulate event times for fixed baseline data and treatment plans
#' @param data Base data (covariates, planned treatment time `s` and `cens_time` are kept).
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM from `fit_dgm()`.
#' @param theta Treatment log-HR used for simulation.
#' @param u Uniforms, one per patient (common random numbers).
#' @return Copy of `data` with simulated `time`, `status`, `trt_time`.
simulate_outcomes <- function(data, dgm, theta, u) {
  checkmate::assert_numeric(u, len = nrow(data), lower = 0, upper = 1)
  X <- dgm_design(data, dgm$covariates)
  eta <- dgm$alpha + drop(X %*% dgm$gamma)
  rho <- dgm$rho
  E <- -log(u)
  # Inversion of the piecewise cumulative hazard: same u gives monotone T in theta
  h_pre <- exp(eta) * data$s^rho
  t_ev <- data.table::fifelse(
    E <= h_pre,
    (E / exp(eta))^(1 / rho),
    (data$s^rho + (E - h_pre) / exp(eta + theta))^(1 / rho)
  )
  out <- data.table::copy(data)
  out[, `:=`(time = pmin(t_ev, cens_time), status = as.integer(t_ev <= cens_time))]
  out[, trt_time := data.table::fifelse(s <= time, s, Inf)]
  out[]
}

Notation: AA = strategy arm, CiaC^a_i = artificial censoring time, Wi(t)W_i(t) = weight of clone ii at time tt, ZiZ_i = censoring-model covariates.

R code: Maringe cloning and weights (R/pipeline.R) 
#' Clone into "surgery within grace" (arm 1) and "no surgery within grace" (arm 0)
#' @param data Patient-level data; @param grace Grace period (days).
#' @return Clone rows: arm, end, event, art_cens.
build_clones <- function(data, grace) {
  ctrl <- data.table::copy(data)[, arm := 0L]
  ctrl[, art_cens := as.integer(trt_time <= grace)]
  ctrl[, `:=`(
    end = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, trt_time, time),
    event = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, 0L, status)
  )]
  surg <- data.table::copy(data)[, arm := 1L]
  # Deaths before grace without surgery stay in the surgery arm (Maringe et al. 2020)
  surg[, art_cens := as.integer(trt_time > grace & time > grace)]
  surg[, `:=`(
    end = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, grace, time),
    event = data.table::fifelse(art_cens == 1L, 0L, status)
  )]
  data.table::rbindlist(list(ctrl, surg))
}

#' Inverse probability of censoring weights for the control arm (Cox censoring model)
#' @param clones Control-arm clones; @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @return Long data split at censoring times, with weight `w` = 1 / P(uncensored at start).
weight_control <- function(clones, spec) {
  f <- stats::reformulate(spec$cens_covariates, response = "survival::Surv(end, art_cens)")
  fit <- survival::coxph(f, data = clones, ties = "breslow")
  bh <- survival::basehaz(fit, centered = FALSE)
  clones[, lp := stats::predict(fit, type = "lp", reference = "zero")]
  # Split at the observed censoring (surgery) times: weights change only there
  ctimes <- sort(unique(clones[art_cens == 1L, end]))
  brk <- unique(c(0, ctimes[ctimes < spec$grace], spec$grace))
  long <- split_clones(clones, brk)
  H0 <- stats::stepfun(bh$time, c(0, bh$hazard))
  # Right-continuous: those censored at a break have left the risk set
  long[, w := exp(H0(pmin(start, spec$grace)) * exp(lp))]
  long[]
}

#' Inverse probability of censoring weights for the surgery arm
#' @param clones Surgery-arm clones; @param data Patient data; @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @return Long data split at grace, with weight `w`.
weight_surgery <- function(clones, data, spec) {
  long <- split_clones(clones, c(0, spec$grace))
  # Censoring happens only at grace end, for patients alive and not yet operated
  alive <- data[time > spec$grace]
  alive[, op := as.integer(trt_time <= spec$grace)]
  f <- stats::reformulate(spec$cens_covariates, response = "op")
  fit <- stats::glm(f, family = stats::binomial(), data = alive)
  alive[, p_op := stats::predict(fit, type = "response")]
  long[, w := 1]
  long[alive, on = "id", p_op := i.p_op]
  long[start >= spec$grace, w := 1 / p_op]
  long[]
}
R code: SynPUF tutorial cloning and weights (R/pipeline.R) 
#' One "start treatment within `win` days" clone set, censored and weighted as in the tutorial
#' @param data Patient-level data; @param win Window (days); @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @return Long data (id, start, stop, ev, w).
ccw_window_arm <- function(data, win, spec) {
  cl <- data.table::copy(data)
  # Tutorial 01: censored at win if followed beyond win without having started
  cl[, nostart := as.integer(time > win & trt_time > win)]
  cl[, `:=`(
    end = data.table::fifelse(nostart == 1L, win, time),
    event = data.table::fifelse(nostart == 1L, 0L, status)
  )]
  long <- split_clones(cl, c(0, win))
  # Tutorial 02: weight 1 in [0, win]; after win, up-weight only recent starters
  after <- long[start >= win]
  model_rows <- rbind(
    cl[nostart == 1L],
    cl[nostart == 0L & time > win & trt_time >= win - spec$recent_days]
  )
  model_rows[, uncens := 1L - nostart]
  f <- stats::reformulate(spec$cens_covariates, response = "uncens")
  fit <- stats::glm(f, family = stats::binomial(), data = model_rows)
  after[, p_unc := stats::predict(fit, newdata = after, type = "response")]
  after[, w := data.table::fifelse(trt_time >= win - spec$recent_days, 1 / p_unc, 1)]
  long[, w := 1]
  long[after, on = c("id", "k"), w := i.w]
  long[]
}
R code: weighted Cox outcome model (R/pipeline.R) 
#' Weighted Cox model for the strategy contrast
#' @param long Stacked long data (id, arm, start, stop, ev, w); @param spec Pipeline spec.
#' @param robust Robust (cluster) SE; FALSE only for large-sample truth runs.
#' @return One-row data.table in the pipeline contract format.
fit_outcome <- function(long, spec, robust) {
  fit <- if (robust) {
    survival::coxph(
      survival::Surv(start, stop, ev) ~ arm,
      data = long, weights = w, cluster = id, ties = "efron"
    )
  } else {
    survival::coxph(survival::Surv(start, stop, ev) ~ arm, data = long, weights = w, ties = "efron")
  }
  est <- unname(stats::coef(fit)["arm"])
  se <- unname(sqrt(stats::vcov(fit)["arm", "arm"]))
  z <- stats::qnorm(1 - (1 - spec$conf_level) / 2)
  data.table::data.table(
    estimate = est, se = se, ci_lo = est - z * se, ci_hi = est + z * se,
    p_value = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(est / se)), n_events = sum(long$ev),
    status = "ok", message = NA_character_
  )
}

A5. True value, calibration and performance measures

  • Truth: ψ(θ)=plim⁡n→∞ψ̂n\psi(\theta) = \operatorname{plim}_{n \to \infty} \hat\psi_n under the outcome-generating model with parameter θ\theta. It is computed as ψ̃(θ)=1R∑r=1Rψ̂N(r)\tilde\psi(\theta) = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R} \hat\psi^{(r)}_N, with N≈50,000N \approx 50{,}000 (copies of the base data) and R=24R = 24; robust SE not needed.
  • Calibration: θ*\theta^* solves ψ̃(θ)=ψ̂obs\tilde\psi(\theta) = \hat\psi_{\text{obs}} (secant search from θ̂\hat\theta, 12 large datasets per step, tolerance 0.005).
  • No-effect scenario: θ=0\theta = 0, so the truth is exactly ψ=0\psi = 0; ψ̃(0)\tilde\psi(0) is a diagnostic only.
  • Performance over B=5,000B = 5,000 replicates: bias =ψ̂‾−ψ= \bar{\hat\psi} - \psi; coverage =B−1∑bI(|ψ̂b−ψ|≤1.96SÊb)= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b - \psi| \le 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b); type I error =B−1∑bI(|ψ̂b|>1.96SÊb)= B^{-1}\sum_b I(|\hat\psi_b| > 1.96\,\widehat{SE}_b) at θ=0\theta = 0. The MCSE of the bias includes the truth’s MC error.
R code: truth and calibration (R/truth.R) 
#' Large-sample truth at one theta
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM; @param data Base data; @param theta Treatment log-HR in the DGM.
#' @param pipeline Pipeline spec; @param cfg Full config (uses `truth`, `seed_truth`).
#' @param n_rep Number of large datasets to average.
#' @return One-row data.table: theta, truth, truth_mcse, n_truth, n_rep.
compute_truth <- function(dgm, data, theta, pipeline, cfg, n_rep = cfg$truth$n_rep) {
  checkmate::assert_number(theta)
  big <- stack_copies(data, ceiling(cfg$truth$n_target / nrow(data)))
  # Same seeds at every theta (CRN), so psi(theta) is smooth for calibration
  seeds <- make_crn_seeds(cfg$seed_truth, n_rep)
  est <- vapply(seeds, function(sd) {
    u <- draw_replicate_rng(sd, nrow(big))$u_event
    run_pipeline(simulate_outcomes(big, dgm, theta, u), pipeline, robust = FALSE)$estimate
  }, numeric(1))
  data.table::data.table(
    theta = theta,
    truth = mean(est),
    truth_mcse = if (n_rep > 1) stats::sd(est) / sqrt(n_rep) else NA_real_,
    n_truth = nrow(big),
    n_rep = n_rep
  )
}

#' Find theta* whose CCW truth equals the observed CCW estimate (paper Step 3)
#' @param dgm Fitted DGM; @param data Base data; @param obs_result Observed pipeline result.
#' @param pipeline Pipeline spec; @param cfg Full config (uses `calibration`).
#' @return List: theta_star, psi_star (search precision), path (search history).
calibrate_theta <- function(dgm, data, obs_result, pipeline, cfg) {
  cc <- cfg$calibration
  psi <- function(th) compute_truth(dgm, data, th, pipeline, cfg, n_rep = cc$n_rep)$truth
  target <- obs_result$estimate
  # Secant search started at the fitted coefficient; psi is smooth and monotone under CRN
  th <- c(dgm$theta_hat, dgm$theta_hat - 0.5)
  ps <- vapply(th, psi, numeric(1))
  for (i in seq_len(cc$max_iter)) {
    if (abs(ps[length(ps)] - target) < cc$tol) break
    n <- length(th)
    slope <- (ps[n] - ps[n - 1]) / (th[n] - th[n - 1])
    th_new <- th[n] + (target - ps[n]) / slope
    th_new <- max(-cc$bound, min(cc$bound, th_new))
    th <- c(th, th_new)
    ps <- c(ps, psi(th_new))
  }
  best <- which.min(abs(ps - target))
  list(
    theta_star = th[best],
    psi_star = ps[best],
    at_bound = abs(th[best]) >= cc$bound,
    path = data.table::data.table(step = seq_along(th), theta = th, psi = ps)
  )
}
